Triggers.value: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Places of worship or religious gatherings

Threat.value: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger

Memory.value: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself
Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish

Negative Appraisals.value: I acted in ways that go against who I am
I am not sure my life is worth living anymore

vignette:
Leilani had been a relief worker in a war-torn region for two years before the attack came. She remembered the dust and the heat, the way the air thickened with smoke, and then—a sudden stillness broken only by the whistle of incoming fire. The convoy had been hit. In the chaos that followed, she found herself pinned beneath rubble, a soldier’s blood warm on her face, and the sharp, sweet smell of his cologne—something expensive, meant for a night off-duty—mixed with the copper of metal and the sourness of fear. She had tried to drag him to cover, but he was too heavy, and she had let go. She had run. That moment, that choice, had never left her.

Now, ten years later, Leilani worked as a park ranger in a sprawling national forest on the Pacific coast. The job demanded solitude and vigilance, and she had sought it precisely because it required both. She knew every trail, every turn, every hidden spring. But her certainty stopped at the park’s boundary. Unfamiliar places—new towns, friends’ homes she had never visited, even the grocery store after a remodel—sent a cold spike through her chest. She would turn the car around rather than enter a parking lot she hadn’t scouted. The world outside the forest felt unpredictable, full of corners where danger could hide.

It was the people that exhausted her most. Visitors came to hike, to picnic, to hug their children. Leilani would watch them from a distance, scanning for signs—a sudden turn, a hand raised too fast, someone walking behind her on the trail. Her body would lock, shoulders tight, breath shallow, until the person passed. She had learned to position herself so that no one could come up from behind. At home, her husband Mark had learned not to touch her without warning. A hug from behind, even a gentle one, felt like the grip of a stranger pulling her into the rubble. She could not bear the press of a body against hers, the warmth that should have been comfort becoming suffocation. She had stopped going to church, too. The smells—the lingering perfume of the woman in the pew ahead, the incense from the altar—took her back to that day in the dust, and she would leave mid-service, shaking.

Her memory of the attack had splintered. Certain moments played with horrifying clarity: the soldier’s cologne, the wet sound of his breath, the weight of the beam across her legs. But the larger story—how she had gotten there, how she had escaped, what happened after—was a tangle of gaps and frayed edges. When Mark asked her to talk about it, she would start, then stop. The thread would slip, and she would find herself saying, “I don’t know, I can’t remember,” even though the images were right there, unbearable. She had come to believe that there was something wrong with her, that she had acted in a way that violated her deepest values—a relief worker who left a wounded man to die. She had no right to belong anywhere anymore. Not among her colleagues, not among her family. Some nights, lying awake while Mark slept, she wondered whether her life was worth continuing at all.

She avoided doctors, both medical and psychological, because the thought of sitting in a small room with a stranger, being asked to describe what she couldn’t describe, felt like a trap. She had not had a physical in four years. She told herself she was fine. But after a hiker’s sudden movement—a boy darting across the trail to greet his mother—sent her dropping to the ground, covering her head, in front of a dozen families, she knew she could not keep the park as her hiding place any longer.

It was Mark who finally drove her to the appointment. Leilani sat in the waiting room, her hands clenched, the smell of coffee and hand sanitizer pressing in. She was terrified of what the therapist would find, terrified of the story she could not tell. But beneath that fear, buried under years of vigilance, was a hope she barely dared to name: that someone might help her stop running.
